entries.why_it_matters: Flood silt seals the surface. Water stands, air is locked out and roots rot. Giving the water a way to leave saves what is still alive.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Push a stick in and pull it out. If the hole fills with water and stays full, or the ground squelches and smells like rotten eggs, the water cannot drain.

entries.why_it_matters: Bare silt bakes hard or washes away with the next rain. Something growing or spread over it keeps the soil in place and lets air in.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Look for open mud with no plants, no stubble and no spread of straw or scraps. Water puddles on it and runs off cloudy.

entries.why_it_matters: Dried land cannot support seed or seedlings. Rain may run off the baked surface instead of soaking in, so the ground stays dry even after it falls.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Dig a hand's depth with fingers or a stick. If the soil is dusty all the way down and a poured cupful sinks in at once and vanishes, there is no water held in it.

entries.why_it_matters: A hard crust turns rain into runoff. Breaking the surface into rough clods lets water soak down where roots can reach it.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Press a spade or stick into the ground. If it bounces or only scratches the top, the surface is sealed and needs breaking open.

entries.why_it_matters: Flushing salt down and out needs a large, steady supply of water. Without enough clean water, the salt stays where it is and crops keep failing.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Check what water you can reach: a well, a stream, a tank or saved rain. If you cannot cover the patch with a hand's depth of water more than once, you do not have enough for flushing.

entries.why_it_matters: Flushing only works if the salty water can leave. With no outlet, the salt circles back to the surface as the water dries.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Pour a bucket of water on the patch. If it sits like a puddle and does not sink or run away by the next light, the water has nowhere to go.

entries.why_it_matters: Roots drown in standing water. Most crops need air around their roots, so the soggy ground must be given a way to shed water.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Look for puddles that stay for days. Step on the ground and watch water rise around your boot. A rotten egg smell means it is airless below.

entries.why_it_matters: Hard packed ground sheds rain and blocks roots. Loosening the top lets water soak in and gives roots a way down.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Drop a cup of water on the flat surface. If it runs off instead of sinking, and a stick will not push in past the first scratch, the ground is packed tight.

entries.why_it_matters: Burnt ground is bare and loose. The first hard rain or a strong wind carries the ash and good soil away, leaving poor ground behind.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Look at the surface. If it is black or grey powder with no living plants and no stubble, and a puff of wind or a splash of water moves it, the cover is gone.

entries.why_it_matters: Sandy soil drains and dries fast and feeds little. Rotting scraps, ash and animal dung help it hold water and food for roots.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Squeeze a damp handful. If it will not hold a ball and crumbles or runs through your fingers, and water sinks away almost at once, it is too loose.

entries.why_it_matters: Clay packs hard and turns sticky or baked. Rotting scraps and dung break it into crumbs that roots can push through and that drain better.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Roll a damp handful between your palms. If it makes a long ribbon or a slick lump without crumbling, it is heavy clay that needs lightening.

entries.why_it_matters: Stony ground holds little fine soil. Without something soft to fill the gaps, water runs through and roots find nothing to feed on.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Sift a handful of the ground. If it is mostly stones with little dark dirt clinging to them, there is not enough soil to hold water and food.

entries.why_it_matters: Debris and spill signs can poison ground and water. Until it is checked, drinking or growing here can harm people and animals.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Look for broken items, drums, glass and oily patches. Smell water in a nearby dip. A sharp or oily smell, or a rainbow sheen, means keep away.

entries.why_it_matters: Sour ground grows thin crops. Knowing which local crops and which treatments suit it saves seasons of failed planting.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Note what grows well without help, such as moss, sorrel and ferns, and what grows poorly. A pinch in baking soda that fizzes well points to sour ground.

entries.why_it_matters: On a slope, bare ground loses its soil to every rain. Cover and barriers slow the water so it soaks in instead of washing the land away.
entries.how_to_spot_it: Look for gullies, exposed roots and a spread of soil at the bottom of the slope. Water that runs off cloudy is carrying your soil with it.
